Trump meets with Iranian officials shortly after threatening annihilation
President Donald Trump and Iranian leaders in New York City for the United Nations General Assembly spoke through an intermediary for hours, taking peace amid war over the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian nuclear weapons aspirations.
Coverage for this event has ended.
Bessent calls Iran regime 'cornered animal,' touts US 'sequencing' strategy
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that the Iranian regime was “cornered” as Washington “sequenced” military, economic and financial pressure.
“They're cornered animals,” Bessent said on Fox News’ “Special Report.”
The Treasury secretary went on to say the results Washington was seeing were the product of what he called “sequencing.”
“The world has never seen anything like this, and it's because of sequencing.
“So we had six weeks of kinetic activity. We have the blockade, and now we have an effort never seen before in terms of constricting and cutting off the financial oxygen to them,” he said of the regime.
“I don't know whether it's going to be a week, a month or two months, but they're going to yell uncle.
“And the goal here can be one of three,” he said before outlining how the outcomes could include the regime turning on itself or an uprising by the Iranian people.
“And then three, to get the Iranians to, if they want to make a deal, to stick to the deal.
“We gave the MoU a try on June 3, and then the Iranians, a few weeks later, began firing on ships in the Strait and being very aggressive. And this time, if there is a deal, I guarantee you they're going to stick with it,” he said.
Oil prices retreat after 4% surge as Iran signals openness to diplomacy
Oil prices fell in early-morning trading in Asia on Thursday after rising 4% in the previous session.
Brent crude futures dipped to 94 cents, or 0.9%, to $102.13 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 59 cents, or 0.7%, to $91.56, Reuters reported.
While Iran said it remained open to diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war, the two sides are far apart on how to reach an agreement, the outlet said.
Zelenskyy sounds alarm on Putin luring foreign fighters into war using 'deception and tricks'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned world leaders Wednesday that Russia is using foreign nationals in its war against Ukraine and urged them not to allow President Vladimir Putin to drag their countries into the conflict.
“We also see people dying on the battlefield who are not Russians,” Zelenskyy said during an address to the United Nations General Assembly.
Explaining how Ukraine regularly receives requests from 47 countries to help recover foreign prisoners of war captured while fighting for Russia, the Ukraine leader said "people from your countries who ended up in Russia through deception and tricks.”
“You know what Russia is doing with your people. It’s your citizens. Take care of them and do not let them end up on another front. Do not let Putin drag you into this war.”
“Do not let Russia put out its fires, cover up its shame and pay for its madness with the lives of your people,” he added.
“Limit his room to act, limit his money, limit his war.”
Zelenskyy also revealed Russia suffered nearly 249,000 battlefield casualties over an eight-month period, including troops killed and seriously wounded.
“These are not just statistics. It’s about people,” he said. “Putin is paying with 248 people for every kilometer. Does anyone still think that he is reasonable and moderate?” Zelenskyy said, referring to Russia’s battlefield losses.
While accusing North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of sending troops to Russia to bolster the Russian military, Zelenskyy said ending the war requires cutting off Moscow’s economic and military resources through sanctions, financial assistance to Ukraine and joint weapons production.
“This ridiculous and never-ending war with Ukraine must be ended,” he said. “I do not know a single world leader who would say otherwise. I do not know anyone who is openly for this war except one man.”
EU leader urges Iran to restore IAEA cooperation, end strikes and reopen Hormuz
European Council President Antonio Costa said Wednesday that he spoke with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and urged him to restore Iran’s cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)
“I stressed that dialogue is the only way to resolve conflicts and ensure lasting peace across the region,” Costa said in a post on X.
“I called for an end to Iran’s strikes against its neighbors and the full restoration of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz,” he added.
Costa said he also urged Iran to resume cooperation with the IAEA, adding that the European Union stands “ready to support all ongoing diplomatic efforts.”
US moving up to 17M barrels of oil a day through Hormuz: Bessent
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that U.S. forces were helping move between 10 million and 17 million barrels of oil a day through the Strait of Hormuz amid the blockade of Iranian ports.
“The tankers, they may get hit,” Bessent said of the conditions in the waterway. “Many of them just sail on,” he added before describing how the Iranians may launch “three, four or five, six drones after them,” he said on Fox News’ “Special Report.”
“Our great Navy is blocking them, but we are getting between 10, 15, sometimes 17 million barrels a day out,” he confirmed.
“To put that in perspective, before the conflict began, the number was 20 and there's probably another 3 million going out through alternate methods.
“So that gets us back to somewhere between 13 and 20, which is the reason we have seen oil come down from the spring highs,” he added.
“And in terms of Operation Economic Outcast, we are squeezing the Iranians like they've never seen,” Bessent said.
Bessent questions how Iran UN delegation will get home as US sanctions squeeze flights
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday he was unsure how Iran’s delegation to the United Nations General Assembly in New York would get home as U.S. sanctions squeezed the country’s international airline operations.
“In terms of Operation Economic Outcast, we are squeezing the Iranians like they've never seen today,” Bessent said on “America Reports.”
“I would say that the external flights from Iran, probably more than 80 or 90% of them, got shut down.
“I'm not sure how the Iranian representatives at the UN are going to get home.
“So we have made it very clear around the world, whether it's the financiers, the people who are doing business to people who are supplying the Iranians, we know who you are, you know who you are, and we are going to prosecute and execute your your companies and your bank accounts every day and every week,” Bessent added.

articles.title_orig: Trump gives Xi Jinping rare airport welcome as summit visit begins
articles.title_zh: Trump gives Xi Jinping rare airport welcome as summit visit begins
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping on Wednesday evening, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to kick off his state visit to Washington.
Xi’s plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 100ft long red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries. US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and first lady Melania Trump traveled to the the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to personally shake Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan’s hands upon their arrival in the US.
It came as Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced that the US and China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called “Busan agreement” – a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies.
Bessent, who met Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would be extended until 10 January, two months after it was due to expire.
The pageantry will continue with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events.
The simmering trade war is one of many thorny issues Trump and Xi must confront during the visit, including the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability during the two-day visit.
On Thursday, the White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to a state dinner being held for Xi.
There was one discordant note in the carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony, when Trump visibly winced at the sound of a US military jet flying overhead as he stood alongside Xi on the red carpet, listening to the US national anthem. Video of the moment showed that while Trump recoiled from the sound of the flyover, Xi remained impassive, as did the wives of both men.
The moment, which was widely mocked online, was captured on a White House livestream but not included in the edited highlights of the ceremony released by Trump’s aides later.
The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, but the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.
Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, instead promoting more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race.
“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.
The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically – further raising the stakes for the US and China.
Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.
Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to honor Xi.
“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”
Robert Mackey contributed reporting

articles.title_zh: Stock futures are flat after soaring Treasury yields trigger a market sell-off: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures were flat early Thursday after surging yields in Treasurys sparked a sell-off in the market and traders anticipated rate hikes from the Federal Reserve.
S&P 500 futures were down 0.31%. Nasdaq-100 futures slipped 0.34%.
During the regular trading day, the S&P 500 slid 0.8%. The Nasdaq Composite lost 1.1% and broke a four-day win streak.
In Asia-Pacific, Japan's Nikkei 225 added 1% following three consecutive days of holiday, while the Topix dropped 0.09%. Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 was 0.76% lower. South Korea's markets are closed for a holiday. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index dropped 0.52%, while mainland China's CSI 300 was down 1.29%.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield, which is tied to rates on mortgages, surged to 5.135% for its highest level since July 2007. The yield on the 2-year note climbed to 4.947% for its highest since May 2024.
As yields surged, so did the market's anticipation of further rate hikes from central bank policymakers. Fed funds futures trading suggests a greater than 68% likelihood that the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee lifts its key rate once more in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool. That compares to a roughly 49% probability just a week ago.
Higher yields tend to squeeze consumers' finances as they face higher borrowing costs at a time when they're already paying more in fuel costs.
Oil prices bounced Wednesday. International Brent crude futures rose about 3.9% to settle at $103.08 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude gained 1.8% to $92.16.
Readings from S&P Global's manufacturing and services purchasing managers' indexes suggested that U.S. businesses are continuing to boom. BMO Capital Markets said in a Wednesday note that even as the results were strong, "severe supply chain bottlenecks," as well as higher fuel and transport prices, can drive inflation.
"Overall, it was a much stronger-than-expected read on US business activity that implies ample latitude for both policy rates and Treasury yields to push higher in the near-term," said Vail Hartman, a U.S. rates strategist at BMO. "If anything, the data reinforces the risk of a renewed acceleration in demand-driven inflation even if supply-side inflation subsides."
Going into Thursday, traders will be watching weekly jobless claims for further details on the state of the economy. On the earnings front, they'll also look for quarterly results from Olive Garden parent Darden Restaurants in the morning and big-box retailer Costco Wholesale in the afternoon.

articles.title_orig: Iowa Judge Dismisses Trump’s Lawsuit Against The Des Moines Register
articles.title_zh: Iowa Judge Dismisses Trump’s Lawsuit Against The Des Moines Register
articles.content_orig:
Judge dismisses Trump's 2024 lawsuit against Des Moines Register over poll results
A judge on Wednesday dismissed President Trump's lawsuit accusing The Des Moines Register and its former pollster of misrepresenting the state of the 2024 presidential race, rejecting the president's claim that the newspaper's poll coverage violated Iowa's consumer fraud law.
Calling the case extraordinary, Iowa District Judge Scott J. Beattie said that allowing the lawsuit and its "faulty" claims to proceed could have a chilling effect that "can discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs." He sided with pollster J. Ann Selzer and the newspaper, who described the lawsuit as a conspiracy theory and an affront to free speech protections.
The ruling Wednesday came hours after a judge heard arguments but did not rule from the bench in a case on Mr. Trump's ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds. Mr. Trump banned the three outlets beginning Friday, assailing what he called "fake news."
Mr. Trump filed the lawsuit against Selzer, The Des Moines Register and the newspaper's parent company in December 2024, accusing them of fraudulently publishing inaccurate poll results to damage him and help Democrats, saying coverage of polls is not protected speech.
Mr. Trump and his team have filed several lawsuits against media organizations accusing them of bias, calling into question the boundaries of free speech protections, particularly for press. Some of those lawsuits have ended in settlements.
In dismissing the case in Iowa state court, Beattie wrote that Mr. Trump's suit sought to "stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability." After hearing the arguments, the judge concluded the constitutional protection "is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed."
Beattie said the case would have to be dismissed even if, solely for the purpose of deciding the motions, he accepted Mr. Trump's team's allegations that the poll was intentionally skewed and its results fabricated. "Even with this assumption, each of the three counts still fails," the judge wrote, because the lawsuit did not meet the legal requirements for fraud or consumer deception. He made clear that the poll and coverage of it are constitutionally protected political speech and not a commercial product.
The White House referred questions to the president's personal lawyers, who did not immediately respond to messages.
Selzer's case was taken up by the free speech advocacy group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression. She said Wednesday she was grateful for the ruling, which "reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference."
"Polling is a social science, not clairvoyance, and no responsible pollster can guarantee an election outcome," Selzer said in a statement.
Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former Iowa state Sen. Brad Zaun, both Republicans, joined the lawsuit. Selzer and her co-defendants wanted the case moved to federal court but, after a year of legal proceedings, the first hearing took place this year in state court.
The poll, conducted by Selzer's company in the final days of October and released just days before Election Day 2024, showed then-Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democrats' presidential nominee, capturing 47% of Iowa likely voters, to Mr. Trump's 44%.
Mr. Trump ultimately won the support of 56% of the nearly 2 million Iowans who voted.
Mr. Trump, Miller-Meeks and Zaun alleged the misleading coverage diminished their reputations, valuable time in the final days of the campaign, and campaign funds and resources.

articles.title_orig: McDonald’s to take on KFC and rivals as Gen Z flock to fried chicken
articles.title_zh: McDonald’s to take on KFC and rivals as Gen Z flock to fried chicken
articles.content_orig:
McDonald’s is betting on fried chicken as health concerns and the rising price of beef shift dining habits.
The company said that it aimed to take an extra 1.5 percentage point-share of the global chicken market by 2030, with an aim to increase its share of drinks by the same proportion. McDonald’s said the growth in chicken, a lower-priced protein, would not come at the expense of beef burger sales, saying it aimed maintain its “leadership position in beef”.
Chris Kempczinski, McDonald’s chair and chief executive, told investors in May that the chain’s share of the chicken market was in the “high teens”, compared with about 45% in beef, but the chicken market was bigger and growing at twice the pace of its red meat counterpart.
McDonald’s has warned that the rising cost of beef, as well as energy, was hitting profits for its franchisees. The chain also faces heavy competition from the rapid rise of chicken shop chains including Popeyes and Wingstop as well as expansion by the more established player KFC, driven particularly by the popularity of fried chicken among younger Gen Z consumers.
“McDonald’s has the unmatched scale, customer insights, brand loyalty and operational capabilities to not only adapt to the next wave of change in our industry, but to turn it into an advantage,” said Kempczinski.
The chain also said it would spend about $8.5bn (£6.4bn) to help franchisees with rent and improve their restaurants.
The change comes amid the rapid rise in chicken shops and sales of chicken and the surging price of beef, which has risen by more than 20% in the past two years in the US and the UK, according to figures from the UK’s Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board.
Peter Backman, an independent food service industry analyst, said “chicken is cheaper and perceived as healthier”.
He said the rising price of beef was likely to be a “drag on the market” for burgers and offering more chicken would enable McDonald’s to sell more to its fans and “steal a bit of market share from other quick service operators”. He said higher drinks sales were probably attractive as beverages tended to be more profitable.
In the UK, 39% of consumers used chicken shops in 2025 compared with 37% in 2023, according to market research firm Mintel, with Gen Z usage hitting 52%, almost matching pizza outlets at 56%. A plethora of other options, including Asian-inspired chains such as Wagamama, are also eating into the market share of burgers and pizza.
Late last year Domino’s Pizza Group announced that its chief executive of two years had stepped down with immediate effect, less than two weeks after he appeared to suggest the UK may be approaching “peak pizza” and that the chain should try to broaden its menu to sell more chicken.

articles.title_orig: Jacoby Brissett: No one has lost confidence in Marvin Harrison Jr.
articles.title_zh: Jacoby Brissett: No one has lost confidence in Marvin Harrison Jr.
articles.content_orig:
Marvin Harrison Jr. hasn’t been the wide receiver the Cardinals thought they were getting when they drafted him fourth overall in 2024. That’s something everyone can agree.
The Cardinals, though, are pushing back against the narrative surrounding Harrison’s slow start to 2026.
A viral video, viewed more than 18 million times, started the discussion about Harrison’s effort level. Other videos have since questioned whether Harrison is giving 100 percent.
Quarterback Jacoby Brissett and coach Mike LaFleur defended Harrison on Wednesday.
“When you talk about his work ethic and you talk about him showing up and being engaged in the meetings and then going out on the field and giving 110 percent and being the Marv we all know he is, that hasn’t changed,” Brissett said, via Tyler Drake of Arizona Sports.
“Nobody’s lost confidence in Marv. The hard part as a young player is the noise from the outside telling you what they expect from you and the things of that nature. Does Marv want the ball? Yes. Do we understand that he wants the ball? Yes. Is it only Week 2? Yes. . . . At some point, the tide will change. When? We don’t know yet. Hopefully soon.”
Harrison has seen four targets, with one catch for 33 yards this season.
LaFleur was asked on Monday about Harrison jogging through routes.
“I don’t see it that way. I think his running style is different from some other people’s,” LaFleur said. “If that’s people’s narrative on him, that’s fine, but I know his teammates don’t feel that way.”
LaFleur doubled down Wednesday.
“In between those walls, Marv is Marv,” he said. “He’s attacking it every single day like he always does, just like his teammates do. I appreciate the way he goes about his business.”
As for whether Harrison’s run-blocking needs to improve, LaFleur said everyone’s “efforts need to improve.”
Dan Graziano of ESPN talked to league executives who wondered whether the Cardinals will shop Harrison before the trade deadline. The Texans are among the teams that could be in the market for help at the position.

articles.title_orig: 8 Navy members attempted suicide on the USS Lincoln during extended deployment, military official says
articles.title_zh: 8 Navy members attempted suicide on the USS Lincoln during extended deployment, military official says
articles.content_orig:
Eight Navy members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have attempted suicide since the beginning of their extended deployment, a top Navy official said in a letter obtained by NBC News.
The length of the deployment, which some service members on board the carrier had described as extraordinarily tough, has raised concerns about supply shortages and the effect on sailors’ mental health.
No deaths have been attributed to suicide during the deployment.
The number of suicide attempts includes those by crewmembers and sailors from the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff; escorting destroyers; and all embarked aviation squadrons, according to the letter, which acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao sent to Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y.
About 7,500 service members, primarily sailors, are part of the strike group.
A Navy official said the letter was delivered to Gillibrand on Tuesday.
The official said the number of sailors who jumped overboard while the Lincoln was in the Middle East providing operations for the war in Iran remains at two, as previously reported. The official did not provide details about the six other attempts.
In the letter, Cao answered a series of questions that Gillibrand, a member of the Armed Services Committee, had asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a previous letter.
The letter also addressed Gillibrand’s concerns about conditions and medical resources aboard the Lincoln.
In a statement, Gillibrand said the conditions on the ship were “serious and deteriorating.”
“Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect,” she said.
President Donald Trump has previously said the deployment was “not nearly long enough.”
The ship was at sea without a port call for 286 days supporting the U.S. war with Iran. A typical deployment is six to seven months, with regular stops to replenish food supplies.
The Lincoln left San Diego in November. Its deployment was supposed to end in May, but it was extended after the war began in February. The ship stopped in Thailand this month and is now sailing back to San Diego after a stop in Guam.
Relatives of those on board raised concerns about food shortages and low morale and how the extended time at sea was “wreaking havoc” on sailors’ mental health, as one relative described it to NBC News last month.
Some military officials have played down or rejected those claims. In an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal last month, Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command, described the concerns as “old news” that were resolved months ago.
This summer, a Navy official said that officials had not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship and that service members’ well-being was a top priority.
“We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise,” the official said in a statement.
The Lincoln has five chaplains, a clinical psychologist, a clinical social worker, behavioral health technicians and an embedded integrated prevention coordination counselor to support the crew, the Navy official said.
If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

WESTLAKE VILLAGE, Calif. (KABC) -- Former child actor Jonathan Taylor Thomas was arrested in Westlake Village on Monday, according to authorities.
The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department said deputies spotted a vehicle stopped at the intersection of Westlake Boulevard and Townsgate Road, blocking traffic at a green light.
Deputies pulled alongside the vehicle to see if the driver needed assistance, and that's when they noticed that the driver appeared to be intoxicated.
While deputies performed field sobriety tests on the driver, the sheriff's department says the passenger of the vehicle -- identified as the "Home Improvement" star, whose legal name is Jonathan Taylor Thomas Weiss -- kept disrupting them.
Authorities said Weiss "appeared intoxicated, continually exited the vehicle and approached the deputies, distracting them from their investigation."
Deputies then attempted to detain Weiss for obstruction and public intoxication, at which point Weiss reportedly kicked a deputy in the stomach.
The former child star was then arrested and booked at the Malibu/Lost Hills Sheriff’s Station.
The driver was also arrested for driving under the influence of alcohol.
So far, no charges have been filed. The sheriff's department said the case will be submitted to the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office for filing consideration.

Dolly Parton's sister Freida defends nephew after firing, restraining order
One of Dolly Parton's sisters is addressing the firing and restraining order against her nephew amid speculation of tension within the family.
She's Alive, LLC (SAL), the entity the late country musician designed to protect her legacy after her Aug. 25 death, filed a lawsuit Sept. 22 alleging her nephew, Bryan Seaver, threatened to smear his aunt’s legacy and made violent threats against several employees. The reported lawsuit and temporary restraining order came a day after Seaver received a termination notice from his role as his late aunt's head of security.
In a brief statement shared on Instagram Sept. 23, Parton's younger sister Freida dismissed the idea of a rift within the family and expressed support for Seaver, her nephew.
"Hi I'll say this and this only: there is no feud within our family. No one among the Parton/Owens family is fighting over Dolly's estate," she wrote. "We all love Bryan, just as we love each other. I love you all!!"
USA TODAY reached out to Seaver through his security company for comment.
Seaver, who oversaw the "Jolene" singer's security operations for more than 20 years, is the son of the late Larry Seaver, who previously held the position, and Dolly's younger sister Cassie Parton, 75.
In addition to working to protect his aunt, her residences and her professional properties, Seaver is the CEO of Squadron Augmented Protection Services, a Nashville-based company offering executive protection, estate security, business intelligence, K-9 services and event security, according to his LinkedIn page.
What is Bryan Seaver accused of?
In a lawsuit filed in Davidson County Chancery Court on Sept. 22, She's Alive LLC (SAL) alleges that Seaver waged a campaign of threats, harassment and intimidation on Parton's family and those entrusted to protect her brand.
Seaver is accused of threatening to ruin Dolly Parton's brand partnerships unless he was paid through podcast appearances and social media, according to the lawsuit obtained by the Nashville Tennesean, part of the USA TODAY Network.
The lawsuit also claimed Seaver made "threats of real-world violence" towards the singer's staff, partners, and legal and business advisers, allegedly often invoking his background as a military contractor during the Iraq War.
"As the entity entrusted by Ms. Parton to protect and promote her life’s work for future generations, SAL must cultivate a safe work environment for employees, advisors, and partners, free from intimidation or hostility — particularly intimidation by an armed former security contractor," the lawsuit reads. "Without relief, Defendants’ calculated campaign will continue to inflict fear, to destabilize SAL’s operations, and to cause further irreparable harm."
The lawsuit said Seaver allegedly told Danny Nozell, the country music legend's former manager who was selected by Parton to run She's Alive, "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or ... pay me."
What has Bryan Seaver said?
In a statement to TMZ shared Sept. 21, Seaver said he and his teams were "dismayed by the unexpected and, so far, unexplained actions" taken by Nozell and Pinnacle Bank.
"We remain unshakably resolved to fulfill her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much," the statement reads.
Seaver announced his aunt's death in an Aug. 25 video shared on social media, saying he first followed Dolly Parton on the road when he was a kid in the early 1980s and got a taste of the doors she opened for her family "to reach the potential we didn't even know was possible." In the video, he said that Dolly Parton personally asked him to reveal her death.
"My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you," he said in the video. "She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD, and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family, whether you liked it or not."
Contributing: Evan Mealins, Nashville Tennessean

articles.title_orig: Trump likely ‘smirked’ as 'crass' Iranian president lashed out at US in UN speech: expert
articles.title_zh: Trump likely ‘smirked’ as 'crass' Iranian president lashed out at US in UN speech: expert
articles.content_orig:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s sharp rebuke of Washington at the United Nations would have drawn little more than a "smirk" from President Donald Trump, who knows he "holds the cards," a foreign policy expert told Fox News Digital Wednesday.
The assessment came after Pezeshkian and Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly in New York from the same podium within 24 hours of one another, trading sharp rhetoric as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to mount.
"Trump understands he holds the cards, and he may not even have paid much attention to what the Iranian president was saying," Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital.
Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of attacking Iran while portraying his country as the victim of aggression.
THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES
"We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists," Pezeshkian claimed.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. America and Israel attacked us."
"I’m sure that would have drawn a smirk or a smile or a chuckle from the president’s face, seeing that crassness," Taleblu said, pointing to what he described as a sharp contrast between Pezeshkian’s rhetoric and the Iranian government’s track record.
Pezeshkian’s address came after Trump used the same U.N. stage to defend the U.S. conflict with Iran and warn that Tehran faces a stark choice between reaching a deal and facing further destruction.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said on Tuesday.
While the rhetoric from both leaders was pointed, Taleblu said their broader diplomatic positions remain largely predictable.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
"To a certain degree, both President Trump and President Pezeshkian’s speeches before the U.N. General Assembly’s 81st session were predictable," Taleblu said.
"Predictable because the status of both countries and their foreign policy toward the other are in a fairly predictable pattern right now."
Despite the threats and recriminations, the two adversaries also appear to be still testing a diplomatic path behind the scenes.
Trump said Tuesday that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spoke with Iranian officials for roughly three hours on the sidelines of the General Assembly and characterized the discussions as productive.
Witkoff later said the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the U.S. and Iranian delegations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also represented Tehran in the discussions, according to reports.
KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL
Both sides, Taleblu said, are attempting "to make time a weapon on their side" and "to put the burden of choosing between escalation and engagement on the other."
But Taleblu went on to characterize Pezeshkian’s broader message as an attempt to cast Iran as a victim through an anti-American, anti-Israel and anti-imperialist framework.
"It seemed to be more of a global South, anti-American, anti-Israeli, kind of anti-colonial, anti-imperialist message that he was looking to kind of paint the Islamic Republic as the victim," Taleblu said.
"In reality, the long-serving victim in this entire crisis is the Iranian people because of the policies of the Islamic Republic."
The competing messages — confrontation from the U.N. podium and diplomacy behind the scenes — highlighted the unresolved tensions between Washington and Tehran as officials explore whether negotiations can produce an off-ramp from the conflict.
TRUMP KEEPS FORECASTING AN IRAN DEAL — WHY THE WHITE HOUSE STILL THINKS IT CAN HAPPEN
"Despite the tough talk at the podium, both sides still feel like they need to signal an interest in talks, even though they’re both trying to use talks to shape an outcome that is more conducive to their interests," Taleblu said.
Pezeshkian also told the General Assembly that Tehran would not surrender to military pressure while signaling that Iran remained open to diplomacy.
"I think the Iranians are trying to signal an interest in talks, but they may run into a brick wall quite soon if they foot-drag or delay or don’t meaningfully provide any kind of substantive change in their policy," Taleblu said, citing Iran’s positions on the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and its nuclear program.
"Ultimately, if the positions remain the same, the fact that they’re oscillating between shooting and talking doesn’t mean much because the red lines haven’t actually moved.

"Of course, the Trump administration is looking for a political win here."

articles.title_orig: Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
articles.title_zh: Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
articles.content_orig:
Meta announced a slate of new wearables during its annual Meta Connect showcase on Wednesday. The star of the event was the new Meta VR Glasses, which pack virtual reality tech into a lightweight smart glasses-style frame with a tethered puck. Meta also announced new pairs of screen-free smart glasses, along with some new AI features and style and frame options.
Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
This year’s Meta Connect featured a new lightweight VR wearable and camera-free Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.
You can catch up on all the highlights from this year’s Meta Connect below.
Meta’s latest wearable offers full virtual reality in a smart glasses-style form factor. Unlike a typical VR headset, the VR Glasses don’t have any straps, and Meta says they’re “five times lighter than Meta Quest 3” at just 100g. Similar to Google’s Project Aura, the glasses are tethered to a pocket-sized puck with the compute hardware, battery, and storage, including a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite, 128GB of storage, and 12GB of RAM. The 5K micro OLED “Infinite Display” has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye, with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
The Meta VR Glasses are launching in spring 2027 for $1,299, pricier than the Meta Ray-Ban Display but less expensive than the Apple Vision Pro, while offering similar features. Users can connect the glasses to a Mac or Windows laptop for use as a virtual external display, with an option for a virtual surface keyboard and touchpad.
The VR Glasses also have access to the full Meta Quest catalog of apps and games and support for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Meta says the glasses are “the first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever,” and users will be able to watch “immersive live sports” with them as well as 3D movies. They even have a “hologram” feature that creates a “photorealistic digital version of your face” for using in calls while wearing the glasses, reminiscent of the “personas” on the Apple Vision Pro.
Meta is launching camera-free smart glasses
The highlight of the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is the feature they don’t have: built-in cameras. You can use them for things like listening to music, taking calls, or chatting with an AI assistant, but they can’t take pictures or record video — features that have sparked privacy and harassment concerns around Meta’s other glasses.
Meta says the new audio-only glasses are also its “lightest, slimmest AI glasses yet,” weighing just 43g. They offer up to 12 hours of battery life per charge, or 48 hours with the charging case. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio will launch on October 13th starting at $349 with 23 different color and lens combinations.
Refreshed Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 arrive with battery and design upgrades
Meta launched an updated version of its main Ray-Ban Meta glasses, starting at $449. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offer up to nine hours of battery life, one hour more than the Gen 2. They also have “a new customizable action button for instant access to Meta AI” and a new six-mic array that Meta says “cuts more than 90% of background noise.”
The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 has a slimmer design than the Gen 2 as well, with 27 color and lens combinations, including new Zena and Aviator frame styles. Notably, one thing that hasn’t changed is the built-in LED light that indicates when the glasses are recording, which Meta rolled out a privacy fix for last month.
Budget glasses launch along with new glasses styles
Alongside its pricier Ray-Ban glasses, Meta also announced some updates to its in-house line of glasses. It’s launching a new lower-cost version of the Meta Adventurer, which will start at $249 for a basic design with black frames and gray lenses, launching October 23rd.
Meta is also introducing a new “Mix & Match” program for customizing its glasses with different frames, lenses, and case colors. Plus, its EssilorLuxottica collection is getting two new styles, Capri and Nova, and the Kylie Jenner Starfire frames are getting a new ivory colorway. Meta’s also launching a new collaboration collection with Lisa of Blackpink.
Meta Glasses are expanding to more countries starting today, too, including Singapore, South Korea, Mexico, and the United Arab Emirates, with availability in Brazil “coming soon.”
Meta Ray-Ban Display is coming to more regions with some new features
A year after they originally launched, the Meta Ray-Ban Display are coming to more regions. The glasses are on sale in the UK and Canada starting today, and they’ll be available in France, Italy, and Germany starting on October 13th. Meta’s also introducing online ordering for customers in those regions and the US.
Meta’s launching a new Explore app for Display glasses where users will be able to “browse and use a growing selection of experiences built for your glasses.” The Meta Ray-Ban Display is also getting photo editing, an improved calendar, and mirrored phone notifications. Plus, Meta says the “hologram” feature launching on its VR Glasses is rolling out on the Meta Ray-Ban Display “in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”
After launching its new Muse assistant earlier this month, Meta says it’s “working on” bringing the AI to its smart glasses. When it arrives on the glasses, Muse will be able to do things like guide your workouts, log meals, book appointments, and “help buy products you see.”
Meta also announced some new features for Muse, including video calls with a customizable live avatar of the AI. Plus, Muse agents are getting their own email addresses for completing tasks and communicating with users.
Meta is making an AI ‘charm’
Mark Zuckerberg teased one last device, Muse Charm, a small AI gadget that houses the Muse agent and looks a little bit like a supersized Tamagotchi. More details will be shared “soon,” he said, but the product is supposed to ship in time for the holiday season.

articles.title_orig: Idaho case may be connected to the 1982 Tylenol murders, officials say
articles.title_zh: Idaho case may be connected to the 1982 Tylenol murders, officials say
articles.content_orig:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- Idaho investigators have identified a man they believe merits further scrutiny in the 1982 Tylenol murders, while acknowledging they have no evidence placing him in the Chicago area when the poisonings occurred.
The Ada County Sheriff's Office on Wednesday identified the man as Dr. Matthew Betkouski, a chemist known as "The Wanderer."
Betkouski, who had a history of mental illness, was found dead by suicide inside a Catholic church in Boise, Idaho, in December 1982. Investigators said their review uncovered comments he allegedly made to co-workers at different points in his career that drew their attention decades later.
Years before the Tylenol killings, Betkouski worked for a fragrance company in Jacksonville.
"Co-workers reported Dr. Betkouski discussing the perfect crime. And how cyanide could be used as a less messy way of taking one's life," Ada County Sheriff's Detective Tim Cooper said.
Investigators said Betkouski later made another similar comment while employed at Lockheed Martin in New Mexico in early 1982.
"Before he was terminated Dr. Betkouski made a comment about how poison could be introduced into over-the-counter capsules if a person wished to do so," Cooper said.
The announcement comes more than four decades after seven people died across the Chicago area after taking cyanide-laced Tylenol capsules. The victims included a 12-year-old child and three members of a single family in Arlington Heights. The deaths prompted the recall and destruction of millions of bottles of Tylenol.
Although James Lewis was later imprisoned on an extortion charge related to the case, authorities never identified him as the person who carried out the killings.
Ada County officials said investigators were able to place Betkouski in Chicago in late 1981, but found no evidence showing he was in the area when the poisonings occurred in September 1982.
"I cannot put his shoes in a pharmacy store aisle 44 years ago. But I also can't dismiss his statements, his actions," Cooper said.
WATCH: I-Team Investigates: The Tylenol Murders
The Chicago Police Department and Arlington Heights Police Department confirmed they have received the investigative file from Ada County and are reviewing the information. Neither agency provided additional details.
The FBI, however, cautioned against drawing conclusions from information that has not been substantiated.
In a statement, the bureau said: "There have been repeated claims over the past 44 years about alleged links to the Tylenol Murders which remain unsubstantiated. Out of respect for the ongoing, legitimate investigation, those impacted by the tragedy, and the law enforcement partners who have provided genuine support since the start, the FBI remains the lead on investigating and releasing credible information to the public once the evidence yields a true case resolution."
Michelle Rosen, whose mother, Mary Reiner, was among those killed in the poisonings, called for transparency and for investigative records to be made public.
"The Unknown Wanderer is not a random name pulled from thin air. He presents as a serious and compelling person of interest whose background merits careful examination," Rosen said in a statement.
The Tylenol murders changed how medications are packaged and are the reason behind the tamper proof bottles we have today.

articles.title_zh: Meta's Zuckerberg says Muse AI agent will take a small fee from transactions
articles.content_orig:
Meta (META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out his plan for monetizing the company's wildly popular Muse AI agent during its Meta Connect conference on Wednesday.
"We believe that Muse will make you money," Zuckerberg told the room full of developers. "And we are standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions."
Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang explained that the company has added support for PayPal and announced integrations with retailers including Walmart (WMT), Best Buy (BBY), The Gap (GAP), Sephora, Wayfair (W), American Eagle (AEO), and others.
On the travel side, Meta is adding the ability to connect with Expedia (EXPE). The company is also bringing grocery shopping to Muse via Instacart.
In addition to laying out the company's plans to monetize Muse, Wang also said the company is rolling out computer control for the Mac, allowing the agent to take over your Mac on your behalf.
Muse is also coming to Meta's Meta VR Glasses, letting you speak to the agent on the go, as well as the company's upcoming Muse Charm, a dedicated handheld device that will allow people to speak to Muse without needing a smartphone or glasses.
While he said engineers are putting the finishing touches on the product, Zuckerberg said it will be available in time for the holidays.
According to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, the Muse app hit 560,000 daily active users after just 11 days.
The app's early success sent Meta stock soaring 11% on Monday, as the market digested the positive news.
While AI agents aren't new, Muse is the first built for the average consumer without requiring any deep technical know-how.
Wall Street analysts are high on Meta's Muse agent, with Wells Fargo and KeyBanc Capital Markets raising their price targets on Meta amid early uptake of the app.
Muse also provides Meta with a clear revenue source outside its standard advertising business, helping drive a return on its vast investments in AI.

articles.title_zh: Meta's Next Smart Glasses Collab Is With Blackpink's Lisa
articles.content_orig:
Meta's next smart glasses collab is with Blackpink's Lisa
Blackpink in your upper-facial area.
Meta introduced its own smart glasses earlier this year as a cheaper option than its Ray-Ban models and a way to partner with celebrities like Kylie Jenner on exclusive designs. The company is building on that strategy at Meta Connect 2026 by partnering with Blackpink rapper Lisa on two different styles of Meta Glasses. It's also expanding its existing offerings and bringing them to more countries.
Both of the "Meta Glasses by Lisa" models feature custom elements, and one of them is a brand new style while the other is an updated take on an existing offering. The Meta Adventurer Lisa Edition are rectangular glasses with a semi-translucent Moonlit Sky frame and Blush lenses, while the new Meta Capri Lisa Edition features a darker, cat-eye frame with grey lenses.
Regardless of which you pick, you'll get a custom frame (complete with a star on the temple tips), a custom charging case with a star design and case charms shaped like Lisa's pets. In terms of the level of customization, these little adornments sound similar to the little piece of bling and mirror bar that the Kylie Jenner version of Meta Glasses feature as well. The same Meta AI, audio and camera features offered on past Meta-branded smart glasses are also available on these special edition models. And as before, they support prescription lenses.
The company is also updating its Meta Glasses by Kylie Jenner collab with a new Ivory (off-white) version of its Starfire frames. Both variants of the Lisa shades and the Kylie Jenner options start at $399. Meta is also selling a new, even cheaper version of the Meta Adventurer frame in black with a plug-in charging case for $249, which is $50 less than the usual $299 starting price for the company's smart glasses. For anyone looking for non-special edition styles, the company is also introducing an entirely new Nova design that shares similarities with Ray-Ban's Headliner style.
Alongside the launch of these new frame options, Meta is also bringing Meta Glasses to more countries. These include Singapore, South Korea, Mexico and the United Arab Emirates today, as well as Brazil in the near future.

articles.title_orig: Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives
articles.title_zh: Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives
articles.content_orig:
A Zoom call on Wednesday with 500 senior Warner Bros staffers to discuss Paramount‘s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit brought by state attorneys general related to its merger with WBD did little to dissipate the gloomy, Mordor-like clouds over the Burbank lot, to use a Lord of the Rings reference.
The video call, which has been routine since Paramount won the $110 billion bid for Warner Bros Discovery, was led by WBD Studios Chief Operating Officer Simon Robinson, who is running point on the merger integration; Chief Legal Officer Priya Aiyar; WBD Chief Comms Officer Robert Gibbs; and HR boss Amy Girdwood. According to sources, the four conceded they didn’t have much visibility into Paramount’s plans for a newly combined company, but indicated that the anticipation is for the deal to close in about 10 days, in line with Paramount CEO David Ellison‘s two-week timeframe he provided Monday.
The name and the leadership structure of the new company will likely be announced ahead of close, the executives reportedly said, though they weren’t clear as to when exactly that might be. We heard that Girdwood told leaders to take a moment to reflect on the great work accomplished during their tenures.
“It feels like a scramble,” one source said.
To say staffers were surprised by the AG settlement Monday doesn’t really cover it.
“It was a big shock,” one person said. “If you were riding the roller coaster, you felt like things were not progressing.”
Still, even if the settlement and its timing came as a surprise, the ultimate result seemed inevitable as WBD CEO David Zaslav has been hellbent on selling the studio. Ellison’s takeover of the cinematic institution founded by Albert, Harry, Sam and Jack Warner “was always bound to happen,” one insider exclaimed.
Zaslav, who is likely to walk away with more than $600 million from the $110B merger, was not on today’s Zoom, we’re told.
The Ellison-run Paramount has said that the Warner Bros acquisition will yield $6B in synergy savings, which don’t necessarily translate into job cuts, but rather by reducing inefficiencies in other structural areas (i.e., real estate portfolios, data servers).
But Warner Bros staffers aren’t buying that.
“We’ve been here before. We know what it looks like,” said one insider about the changeover in ownership of Warner Bros over the past decade. It was only four years ago that AT&T dumped WarnerMedia into the hands of Discovery.
Myriad people inside Warner Bros are cynical about the capping of severances and the fact that only a few at the top are bound for a post-merger windfall. There’s also ire over the pausing of contract renewals due to the acquisition, as well as irritable infighting between departments about theatrical failures this year: No one WB title has cleared $100M at the domestic box office, with the highest-grossing movie stateside being Wuthering Heights at $84M. Home entertainment and data analytics divisions were none too happy about DC’s Supergirl tanking; with its $186M net production cost and a global box office gross of $126.3M, key staffers believe DC Studios chose the wrong comic book character to adapt.
On the immediate horizon as the Paramount-Warner Bros marriage comes together is Digger, the $125M political satire starring Tom Cruise, directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu and produced by Legendary. It opens on October 2. While domestic debut prospects are at around $20M, Warners is hoping to get past any sour headlines about box office-to-cost ratios on the film, much like it did on One Battle After Another, as the four-time Oscar-winning filmmaker’s Doctor Strangelove-like epic is being primed as an awards-season contender. It is a chip Paramount really doesn’t have on its year-end schedule.
The new Paramount could also inherit another awards contender and its first billion-dollar-grossing title since Skydance took over the Melrose Ave lot with Legendary/Warner Bros’ Dune: Part Three. That opens on December 18.
At Paramount, the latter epic would fall into the arms of global marketing and distribution guru (and former WB senior ranking theatrical suit) Josh Goldstine, who led the Dune franchise across two movies to a $1.12B global gross and eight Oscars.
We’ve heard on the Paramount side that it’s still TBD in regards to how the merger will handle duplications in marketing and distribution.
“There could be more fear on the Paramount side,” says one source in the know when it comes to marketing. How’s that? Goldstine will be back together with the team he built at Warners, meaning Dana Nussbaum and Christian Davin in global marketing along with Creative Advertising EVP John Stanford.
There’s also a thick fog around those staffers who were bound to decamp from Warner Bros proper in the previously planned Gunnar Wiedenfels-led Global Networks spinoff.
Yes, Warner Bros staffers are already putting themselves out there for other jobs. Some of them have already found new gigs: Former EVP Comms Katie Martin Kelly, prized by Warner Bros Motion Picture group co-heads Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, high-tailed it for Netflix as her contract ended, rather than wait for the Russian roulette the new conglomerate could bring. Former HBO Max EVP Originals Marketing Pia Barlow found a new job at Amazon MGM Studios as their Series Marketing VP, a gig that triggered WBD to sue for poaching.
The merger closing will likely trigger more voluntary departures as many WBD executives had been waiting to cash out stock options post-transaction, no longer bound by contracts that typically provide a way out in case of change of ownership.
“Since David Zaslav took control of Warner Bros, there’s just been thousands of jobs lost,” one former Turner publicist emphatically told us. “Those are jobs that the entertainment industry is never going to get back.”
And therein lies the ultimate piercing wound for any Warners or Paramount employee in the danger zone: The fact that there are not a lot of jobs out there is a big deal.
What’s more, adds a source, “People are very concerned about the survival of the Warner Bros brand.”
Counters a senior ranking insider at the conglomerate: “There’s a feeling of relief from senior executives to junior staff about the possibilities that the new company can bring. They were very excited by David Ellison’s note.”
For now, Paramount is inheriting at least 39 Warner Bros theatrical releases on the calendar dated between October 2 this year and the end of 2028. That output reps 56% of what will be a currently combined 70 features between the two studios. During the agita of Netflix and Paramount courting Warner Bros, the studio’s greenlighting of productions has been at a loud hum; assumptions were made by some that Warner Bros Motion Pictures would be in purgatory during merger talk time, and that filmmakers and reps would be wary of taking projects to them. That’s not really an option for content creators at a time when it’s a miracle for any major motion picture to get off the ground.
Something to look forward to: While a Barbie sequel hasn’t been greenlit due to ongoing talks with top-tier talent including director Greta Gerwig and stars Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, expect that to be one of the first orders of business for the new Ellison-owned Paramount-Warner Bros.
Beams one optimistic Warner exec, “The new merger gives us the all the financial resources to compete on a level with the big streamers.”

articles.content_orig:
US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
A US judge has temporarily blocked the deportation of a Venezuelan man who was shot by immigration agents in Texas, his lawyer says.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, is being held in a detention centre with a bullet in his back, according to his lawyer. Judge Orlando Garcia, a Clinton appointee, scheduled a hearing for Garces Perez to appear in court in person next week.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement that an "illegal alien" had been the subject of a targeted vehicle stop but pushed back against suggestions he had been given inadequate medical care.
The incident comes months after a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man in Houston.
Garces Perez's immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, has filed a federal lawsuit for a temporary restraining order to prevent his removal from the country.
Since the judge ordered that her client appear in person on 30 September, he cannot be deported before then, she said.
"For now, we have secured a temporary block on his deportation while his case moves forward," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote on social media.
"This is an important step, but our work is not over," she wrote. "Wilber still needs appropriate medical care, and we will continue fighting to protect his rights."
The gunshot fractured his clavicle and he is wearing a sling while having "significant swelling and pain," Lincoln-Goldfinch said.
The cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced has not yet been determined, she said.
A spokesperson for US Attorney's Office in Texas declined to comment on the case.
The ICE agent who shot him - who joined the agency last year - was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting, sources told the BBC’s US partner CBS News.
The Austin Police Department released footage from officers responding to the scene, but did not show what led to the incident.
On Tuesday, DHS pushed back against what it called "false narratives" surrounding what had happened, blaming sanctuary cities and media for "spreading lies" and discouraging people from resisting officers and evading arrest.
"Contrary to their claims, this person is an illegal alien who has no legal status to be here and has been given some of the best medical care he's ever received in his life," said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a statement to the BBC.
DHS said the man, whom they did not name, was "the subject of a targeted vehicle stop" and that his work permit expired last year.
"No amount of smears and false narratives will slow down ICE from doing its job by removing dangerous illegal aliens from our communities and making America safe again," Mullin said.
The Austin Police Department, which was not involved in the incident, released dashcam and body camera footage on Tuesday showing its officers at the scene.
It does not show the shooting, but several gunshots can be heard in one dashcam clip, while another shows officers approaching Garces Perez's car and detaining him. At one point, Garces Perez's t-shirt is cut to reveal what appears to be a single gunshot in his back.
Lincoln-Goldfinch previously told the BBC that after being unable to move his arm in the detention facility, Garces Perez was taken back to hospital on Monday evening. He was treated there and has since been returned to the detention facility.
He said he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during his transfer, despite his injury, she said.
Lincoln-Goldfinch added that detention personnel had revoked his communication privileges and moved him from an infirmary into an isolated room with a flat, non-adjustable bed.
In its statement on Tuesday, DHS said Garces Perez had received medical care "around the clock" and denied claims he received no pain medication and was forced to sleep on the floor.
"This alien was released from the hospital and arrived at the detention facility just a few hours later, where he slept on a bed," DHS said.
Texas lawmaker Joaquin Castro, a Democrat, on Tuesday demanded the Venezuelan national's release from detention.
Local and state officials have pushed for an independent investigation into the shooting, which occurred just before on Sunday afternoon.
Hours later, dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave the city.
DHS said on Tuesday that ICE "will not be slowing down nor leaving Austin".
The man's lawyer told US media he was making a DoorDash delivery when an unmarked black truck sideswiped his car.
He did not know the truck was an ICE vehicle and made a U-turn, she said. His car was hit again before agents got out and shot him, according to the attorney.

articles.title_orig: US rejects pleas from OpenAI, Anthropic for global AI standards
articles.title_zh: US rejects pleas from OpenAI, Anthropic for global AI standards
articles.content_orig:
US rejects pleas from OpenAI, Anthropic for global AI standards
The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have told the UN that the current pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development, and the risks it poses to society, demands international coordination.
Altman called for common risk evaluation standards, as did Dario Amodei of Anthropic, a main rival of OpenAI, and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face.
Earlier this month, Amodei wrote an essay welcomed by Altman and others calling an AI development slowdown in response to fears about the technology's threat to humanity.
However, at the same UN conference, a key technology advisor to US President Donald Trump, rejected the idea any new form of AI regulation.
Michael Kratsios, a former Scale AI executive, admitted that the speed of AI development is increasing and that there are risks presented by the technology, but told the UN this was not reason enough "to pause development or constrain it with new global governance structures".
"International dialogue in this forum and others cannot be allowed to drift toward global governance," Kratsios added.
Kratsios's comments echoed similar statements made by Trump in recent weeks.
Trump told the UN on Tuesday he wanted to rebrand it "super intelligence" and has strongly opposed any idea of an AI slowdown because of the US's competitive advantage in the sector.
"We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins," he said earlier this month.
Sam Altman of OpenAI and other AI chief executives expressed a different view in their talks to the UN on Wednesday.
"If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," said Altman.
He told the UN that he wanted countries to start working together toward "the collective good in the face of powerful new technology".
He called for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained.
He also called for "speedy incident reporting, classification, and reporting protocols so the world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes".
"We need common standards so countries can compare evidence, verify compliance, and have a shared language and understanding what is happening," Altman added.
Anthropic's Amodei and Hugging Face's Delangue made similar comments in their speeches.
Amodei said that AI "if managed poorly... could be a risk to humanity as a whole".
He added that further development of AI tools calls for "even more stringent standards of safety".
"We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei added.
"But regardless of what we do, managing these risks is ultimately bigger than any one company, and it has an industry-wide and global scale."
Hugging Face's Delangue said: "The global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure."
All three of the executives are based in the US and directly involved in the development of AI technology.
Hugging Face, a platform for AI developers, more recently rose to prominence after it admitted to being hacked by AI agents, or AI bots that operate somewhat autonomously, that came out of OpenAI.
Hugging Face has since been acquired by AI chipmaker Nvidia.
The Hugging Face hack has been treated as a 'wake-up call' within the industry for the ways in which AI technology has advanced and could hypothetically act in ways that could harm humanity.

articles.title_orig: Giants' Jaxson Dart to undergo knee surgery that will end his 2026 season
articles.title_zh: Giants' Jaxson Dart to undergo knee surgery that will end his 2026 season
articles.content_orig:
The New York Giants' fears have been realized. Quarterback Jaxson Dart will undergo knee surgery that will end his 2026 season, Giants coach John Harbaugh announced on Wednesday. Harbaugh left the door open for a potential postseason return. According to ESPN, Dart's ACL is intact, but the second-year signal-caller suffered damage to his MCL, PCL, and meniscus. The meniscus is reported to be the main issue.
Dart suffered the injury on the first drive of the night in New York's Monday night matchup against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 2. The former first-round pick was hit by multiple defenders while in the air, and his knee bent awkwardly. Initially, it was thought Dart's injury was not as severe, with reports suggesting he sprained his MCL.
Upon further review of the injury, however, it was worse than initially diagnosed.
Starting 12 games as a rookie after being the No. 25 overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, Dart entered this season as the full-time starter, and New York was eyed as a potential breakout team with John Harbaugh as head coach. The club furthered that offseason hype when it defeated the Dallas Cowboys in the season opener. In that game, Dart completed 79.3% of his passes for 230 yards and three passing touchdowns. Now, the 2026 season is viewed through a much different lens.
With him on the shelf, the Giants will likely turn to Jameis Winston as their starter going forward. While coming in under duress on Monday night against the Rams, Winston completed 11 of 27 passes for 111 yards and an interception.
That sharpens the stark contrast in what the play under center has looked like for New York over the last two seasons, with and without Dart.
Over the next month-plus, the Giants will host the Tennessee Titans in Week 3, and then the Arizona Cardinals in Week 4 before heading to Washington to face the Commanders (who lost their starter in Jayden Daniels) in Week 5. They'll return to MetLife Stadium for a Week 6 matchup against the Saints, then travel to Houston to face the Texans in Week 6 before their Week 7 bye.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Ban of News Organizations Goes Beyond Obama, Biden Actions
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Ban of News Organizations Goes Beyond Obama, Biden Actions
articles.content_orig:
In banning CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, the Trump administration has argued that the move is similar to actions taken by Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden. But the ban goes beyond what those presidents did.
In a Sept. 21 press release, three days after President Donald Trump said the news organizations would be barred “effective immediately,” the White House said that “[a]ccess changes are nothing new,” and that “Democrat Administrations have restricted, punished, and locked out the press” for “years.” The release listed several examples of incidents involving the press during the Obama and Biden administrations.
“There’s no basis to suggest that Biden and Obama ‘did it too,'” Ken Paulson, director of the Free Speech Center at Middle Tennessee State University, told us. “Trump’s action is singular and unprecedented,” he said, noting that Trump has instituted a “full ban of multiple news media” and “is targeting news organizations because they are publishing content he finds unflattering.
“That violates the First Amendment prohibition against government using its power to punish ideas,” Paulson said.
Trump announced the ban on Sept. 18 in a post on Truth Social, saying it was due to reporting what he called “FAKE NEWS.” When questioned by reporters later that day, Trump repeated that he was doing this “because they’re fake news.” He said the news organizations “purposely write negative news” in order to “try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration.”
We’ll explain what happened in some of the instances under Obama and Biden cited in the White House press release and by other Republicans. First Amendment experts told us that Trump’s ban is different.
Amy Kristin Sanders, a professor of First Amendment studies at Penn State University, told us that Trump’s action was “unprecedented,” “particularly when taken in light of President Trump’s public stance about why he banned the news organizations.”
“What the Trump Administration has done is revoke access for news organizations that have already been granted press access while publicly saying it is because President Trump doesn’t like the way he is being covered by those news organizations,” Sanders told us in an email. “These outlets are being targeted specifically because they engaged in critical coverage.”
Aaron Terr, director of public advocacy at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, which defends free speech rights on college campuses and elsewhere, said, “Past presidents have limited outlets’ White House access based on hostility toward their reporting. For example, the Nixon administration, displeased with the Washington Post’s coverage of Watergate, barred one of the paper’s reporters from covering White House social events.” And the Obama administration initially excluded Fox News from a TV reporting pool for one interview (we’ll explain that incident below).
“But I don’t know of any past example of a president indefinitely banning a media outlet from the White House,” Terr told us.
The White House press release defended the president’s ban. “The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool,” the release said.
Terr disagreed. “Just last year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit reaffirmed that when the White House opens its facilities to the press generally, it cannot exclude reporters based on disapproval of their views,” he said, calling the action a violation of the First Amendment.
CNN, Politico and MS NOW sued the administration, asking a federal judge to block enforcement of Trump’s ban and to restore their access to the White House. Administration officials responded in a court filing saying that the news organizations “have failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum'” by “‘publishing sensitive or classified information.'” A hearing was held Sept. 23.
In response to Trump’s action, the other major TV networks said they wouldn’t participate in pool coverage of the president’s events.
In its press release, the White House highlighted a feud between the Obama White House and Fox News in 2009, early in Obama’s presidency. The Obama White House questioned whether Fox News was a legitimate news organization and excluded “Fox News Sunday” when the president made the rounds on all of the other Sunday news talk shows. And the Treasury Department reportedly tried to limit access for Fox News to an interview with an administration official.
“In 2009, the Obama White House attempted to exclude a Fox News reporter from an interview with an unpaid executive pay consultant for the U.S. Treasury Department. Other news organizations objected to the effort and supported Fox and it never occurred again,” Paulson told us. “Continuance of this practice would have raised significant First Amendment questions.”
In a Sept. 19 talk at Colgate University, Obama commented on Trump’s ban on certain news outlets. “I’m trying to think what would’ve happened if I had said, ‘You know what, Fox News, you’re out of here.’ It’s unimaginable.” Obama didn’t kick out the network from the White House. But his administration took other actions against Fox News, and the Justice Department also surveilled one of the network’s reporters as part of aggressive measures to curtail leaks to the media.
We wrote about these actions in 2018, when Obama said he had “complained plenty about Fox News, but you never heard me threaten to shut them down or call them enemies of the people,” a reference to Trump repeatedly calling the media that. As we said then, Obama did more than complain. He didn’t use the phrase “enemies of the people,” though he did say that Fox News’ “point of view” was “ultimately destructive” to the U.S.
On Sept. 20, 2009, Obama appeared on the Sunday talk shows on NBC, CBS, CNN, ABC and Univision, but ignored “Fox News Sunday.” Asked about the snub, White House spokesman Josh Earnest criticized Fox for not airing Obama’s Sept. 9, 2009, joint address to Congress on healthcare. The speech did air on the Fox News Channel, however — but not the broadcast network. Obama didn’t make it to “Fox News Sunday” until his last year in office.
In October 2009, the White House ramped up its rhetoric. Anita Dunn, the White House director of communications, told the New York Times, “We’re going to treat them the way we would treat an opponent” and said that “we don’t need to pretend that this is the way that legitimate news organizations behave.” When asked about Dunn’s comments, White House senior adviser David Axelrod said that “it’s not just their commentators, but a lot of their news programming, it’s really not news. It’s pushing a point of view.” He added, “We’re going to appear on their shows. We’re going to participate, but understanding that they represent a point of view.”
That same month, the Treasury Department reportedly tried to exclude Fox News from a pool TV interview of an administration official, Kenneth Feinberg, the so-called “pay czar.” The White House disputed that account, saying the issue was merely a miscommunication. But Fox News and other news outlets reported that the Treasury Department had tried to leave Fox News out of the pool, until the other TV networks protested. “All the networks said, that’s it, you’ve crossed the line,” CBS News White House correspondent Chip Reid told his own network.
Fox News did interview Feinberg.

Of course, none of that justifies what the Trump administration is doing now. Two wrongs don’t make a right.
